public_rationale: An older AI-researcher survey reported a 5% median for extremely bad outcomes, above Marcus's approximately 3%. That is relevant context, but it does not establish what most AI industry people believed in July 2025. The searched surveys do not match both the population and period, and the meaning of doom also varies.
limitations: A researcher sample is not automatically representative of the AI industry.
Older beliefs cannot be assumed unchanged.
Different catastrophic outcomes and time horizons produce different probability estimates.

from_speaker: still lower than most industry people’s
our_interpretation: Treat approximately 3% as Marcus's stated comparison value, rather than independently assessing his private belief.
Read 'most' as more than half of people working in the AI industry, rather than a selection of prominent executives or safety researchers.
Compare estimates of substantially equivalent catastrophic outcomes under comparable time horizons.
Read the ongoing comparison as an early-July 2025 snapshot before publication. Older expert surveys are context unless evidence establishes that they represent this population and period.
criteria.support_condition: A suitably representative contemporaneous survey establishes that more than half of AI industry people assigned a probability above approximately 3% to a comparable doom outcome.
criteria.contradiction_condition: A suitably representative contemporaneous survey establishes that no more than half assigned a probability above approximately 3%, with uncertainty small enough to distinguish the majority threshold.

evidence.explanation: The result makes Marcus's comparison plausible for this older research sample. It does not establish the distribution among AI industry people in July 2025, and the question conditions on advanced AI.
Pew explicitly cautions against generalizing its expert sample to all experts. Its 2024 fieldwork also does not measure the July 2025 comparison.
